The Hugo Award process has always been hackable, There was just never anyone narcissistic enough to hack it.

With about 24 hours left to the Hugo Awards it is becoming increasingly unclear if the Sad Puppy Slate will or will not succeed in awarding science-fiction's highest honors to a slate of (mostly) mediocre B-listers in the field. The issue has received enough attention that NPR did a story on it this week. Last week George RR Martin decided to weigh in with an in-depth essay about the Puppy's complaints and its merits or lack thereof.

Charlie Jane Anders from Gawker's IO9 suggests the Puppies success in stuffing the nomination ballot this year in fact disproves their very basis for existing: "The Beale strategem (sic) only succeeds if all the other nominations are scattered and disorganized. And that kind of disorganization is exactly what we saw in most nominations. It appears that everybody except Bealeâs crew simply nominated whatever stories they happened to enjoy in 2014. Had there been a secret left-wing bloc nominating its own stories in lockstep, then Bealeâs strategy would have failed."
The Hugo Award process has always been hackable, There was just never anyone narcissistic enough to hack it.

I'm not entirely sure that GRRM is using some terms in the same way I'm familiar with (and since I'm a tech and he's a pop fantasy author I'd probably defer to him.) For instance, describing Ursula LeGuin as "the field's most eloquent and respected feminist for decades" is something I can endorse. Calling her a SJW (unless the meaning of this term has changed a LOT) I cannot.

So IO9 has repeated the claim that the Sad/Rabid Puppies believe they are fighting a coordinated left-wing conspiracy? Color me surprised. No Chuck Anders, while I'm sure you can find members of those movements who do believe that, the consensus opinion, and the stated opinion of the movements' leaders, is that they are fighting a group of ideologues whose beliefs happen to align. It's almost like IO9 did not seek comment from Larry Correia, Brad Torgersen, or Theodore Beale before publishing.
